China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

Rwanda needed patience to break Sudan’s resistance.

KIGALI – Rwanda secured a place in the semi-finals of the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations CECAFA zonal qualifiers after overcoming Sudan 2-0 in an intense last group-stage game setting up a date with Somalia on Saturday.

Uganda and Ethiopia also advanced from a decisive day of at Kigali Pelé Stadium.

Rwanda needed patience to break Sudan’s resistance before a spectacular free-kick from Pacifique Bahati gave the hosts the lead late in the first half.

Substitute Valentin Tuyizere then scored with his first touch in stoppage time to seal the victory and send the junior wasps into the last four.

The result brought relief to Head Coach Jimmy Murisa, whose team had spent much of the match creating opportunities without converting them. More importantly, it ended Rwanda’s long wait to reach the semi-final stage of the regional competition.

“We’re happy to be in the next phase, the semi-finals. I’m very happy, because it’s been a while without progressing to the semi-finals. The next assignment is to focus against Somalia on Saturday, and we believe it’s even possible to lift the trophy,” Murisa said after the match.

Pacifique Bahati gave the hosts the lead late in the first half.

Rwanda signaled their intentions from the opening whistle, with Kevin Munyembarag appearing to score inside the first minute before the goal was ruled out because the ball had crossed the perimeter line.

Pacifique Niyompano tested Sudan goalkeeper Mustafa Ahmed from outside the penalty area in the seventh minute, while five corners in the opening 10 minutes illustrated the pressure Rwanda were applying.

Yet Sudan held their shape, frustrating the hosts despite Rwanda’s possession and repeated attempts to find an opening.

Irene Mugisha received a yellow card approaching the half-hour mark, but the breakthrough remained elusive until deep into first-half stoppage time.

A foul on Pacifique Bahati just outside the penalty area presented Rwanda with a promising free-kick. Bahati himself took responsibility, sending the ball over the defensive wall and bouncing into the net off the crossbar.

The goal changed the complexion of the contest, but it did not end Sudan’s resistance.

Head Coach Jimmy Murisa is determined to beat Somalia on Saturday.

Rwanda continued to attack after the interval, spending much of the second half in the opposition’s territory, while Ahmed made a series of important saves to keep his team in contention.

Rwanda missed several opportunities, including a late chance for Zaidi Niyonzima after the goalkeeper had been drawn out. But with the final whistle approaching, Tuyizere came off the bench and scored two minutes into added time, settling the contest at 2-0.

Murisa acknowledged that his players still need to improve their finishing, although he considers their ability to create chances an encouraging sign.

“If you create chances, it’s easy maybe to miss. But if you create more chances, it’s a good sign that things are going well,” he said.

He added that the team would work on its composure in front of goal before the semi-final, while continuing to help players manage the expectations that come with competing in a major regional tournament.

Somalia secured their place in the semi-finals with a 2-0 victory over Kenya.

Somalia secured their place in the semi-finals with a 2-0 victory over Kenya, producing a disciplined performance before delivering two decisive goals.

Mahmud Osman broke the deadlock in the 41st minute, giving Somalia an advantage they carried deep into the second half. Abdullahi Hashi then scored a superb free-kick in the 84th minute to double the lead and confirm the victory.

The result set up Saturday’s encounter with Rwanda, bringing together two teams that have demonstrated an ability to withstand pressure and produce decisive moments.

Murisa described Somalia as a strong opponent, praising their passion and style of play, but insisted Rwanda would approach the contest with confidence.

“We respect them, but we also have our mission and what we want to achieve. I hope to see us get through to the next phase,” he said.

Uganda and Ethiopia, who played out a 1-1 draw in their last group encounter.

The other semi-final will feature Uganda and Ethiopia, who played out a 1-1 draw in their last group encounter.

After a tightly contested opening period, Ethiopia took the lead through Zemicheal Minyahel Niguse. Uganda responded five minutes later when Arnold Kayemba finished a well-worked move from midfield, ensuring the points were shared.

The draw leaves the two teams preparing for another meeting with considerably more at stake, with each hoping for a place in the final.

Urukiko rw’Ibanze rwa Kicukiro rwaciye Ishimwe Vestine ihazabu ya 200.000 Frw nyuma yo gusubika urubanza Idrissa Ouedraogo yamurezemo, kubera ko inyandiko y’ivuka ry’umwana wagombaga gukorerwa isuzuma rya ADN itashyizwe muri sisitemu.

Ni icyemezo cyafashwe kuri uyu wa 14 Ukwakira 2026, ubwo urukiko rwasubikaga uru rubanza kugira ngo habanze hatangwe inyandiko y’ivuka ry’uwo mwana.

Umucamanza yavuze ko kudashyira iyo nyandiko muri sisitemu bitinza iburanisha, kuko yari ikenewe kugira ngo hagenzurwe amakuru y’umwana wasabiwe gukorerwa isuzuma rya ADN.

Urukiko rwaciye Ishimwe Vestine ihazabu ya 200.000 Frw, ruvuga ko ibyabaye bifatwa nko gutinza urubanza.

Urubanza rwimuriwe ku wa 21 Ukwakira 2026, saa Tanu za mu gitondo.

Idrissa Ouedraogo yareze Ishimwe Vestine, asaba ko urukiko rutegeka uyu mugore kumwereka umwana avuga ko babyaranye, ndetse rugategeka ko hakorwa isuzuma rya ADN hagati ye n’uwo mwana.

Ibi bikubiye mu kirego Idrissa Ouedraogo yatanze mu Rukiko rw’Ibanze rwa Kicukiro ku wa 17 Nzeri 2026, nyuma yo guhakana ibyo Ishimwe Vestine yari aherutse kumurega asaba gatanya.

Ouedraogo yavuze ko kuva umwana bivugwa ko yabyaranye na Ishimwe Vestine yavuka, atarigera amubona, nubwo yakomeje gusaba ko amwerekwa.

Ishimwe Vestine ni we wabanje kurega asaba gutandukana burundu na Idrissa, avuga ko yabitewe n’ibibazo byavutse amaze kumenya ko afite abandi bagore.

Mu nyandiko ye, Idrissa ahakana ibyo ashinjwa, avuga ko ibyo Vestine ashingiraho asaba ubutane bitigeze bibaho.

Urubanza Idrissa Ouedraogo aregamo Ishimwe Vestine rwasubitswe

The F1 race in Rwanda is already being used to promote the country's Visit Rwanda tourist brand

Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".

The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".

For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.

However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.

Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.

Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.

President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.

"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.

South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.

"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.

"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?

The new track near Kigali has been designed to exploit Rwanda's natural landscape

The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.

F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.

The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.

Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.

Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.

"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.

"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."

Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.

But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.

"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.

"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."

South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.

"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.

"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."

Visit Rwanda announced a multi-year deal to become the main sponsor of Premier League club Aston Villa in July

Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.

Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.

The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.

Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.

However, the tourism brand then became the front-of-shirt sponsor of fellow Premier League club Aston Villa.

Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.

"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.

"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."

The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.

"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."

F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.

F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.

A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."

However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".

"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.

When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.

"I honestly don't care about what they say."
